cells.tense: You are here with the pen, and what you held together has held.
cells.act: rest in the result of the tending
cells.ask: Sit with one thing your group still does that you helped keep alive, and give it ten minutes without touching a single part of it.
cells.core:
What you carry in this group has been tested, and it held. You've stayed with the practice long enough to know which parts still feed people and which just kept the clock ticking, and what survived that is yours by choice now, not by habit. The thing you kept going does not need your hand on it every week.

Care that doesn't exhaust is care you can keep giving. So use what's grown: sit with one thing you helped keep alive and leave the room as it is. See what people take from it, yourself included. The work of holding it is finished for now, and what's left is the part that's easy to skip — enjoying the result before you turn to the next thing that needs rescuing.

cells.tense: You are bracing for whether it holds next year, and that year cannot be written yet.
cells.act: give directions plainly, once, and let them walk
cells.ask: The next time someone in the group asks how a thing is done, answer once, plainly, then walk off and don't circle back.
cells.core:
The commitment has gone into overdrive: you're not only keeping the practice alive, you're rehearsing its future by yourself. Who might leave, what the group looks like in a year, whether anyone will still care — all of it decided in advance, alone, in your head. A loyalty run this hard stops being about the thing and starts being about holding every version of it at once.

Practice works better without force, and so does loyalty. Hand the route over once and walk off. You'll learn what actually holds because they held it, not because your hands stayed on it — and the planning can stop running in front of the year you're standing in.
cells.sheetLine: You're bracing against a year you can't write.
cells.verb: carrying a commitment through friction until only what's chosen remains
cells.place: in what a group keeps going and hands on

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door the group has already walked through.
cells.act: give a concrete piece of help and finish it
cells.ask: Find one person in the group who needs a specific piece of help, carry it through to done, then tell them it's finished.
cells.core:
You know how a group holds a practice steady, and right now you're at the edge of it with your hands full, watching other people carry what you used to carry. The commitment isn't gone. It just isn't reaching anything it can land in, and the hours you spend staying ready don't count as giving.

Start smaller than feels right. Find one person inside the shared thing you both care about who needs a finite piece of help, and finish it, then say so and stop. Strength shared in that size is small enough to hold and real enough to feel, and the current comes back through you because it finally has somewhere to go.
cells.sheetLine: You're still at the door they've walked through.

cells.tense: You are keeping this going by hand while calling it how it has always been done.
cells.act: let the abundance be seen and used
cells.ask: When the group uses something you quietly kept going, skip the remark that it's nothing, and for one week leave the credit where it sits.
cells.core:
Someone remembers the words, notices what's fraying, and renews it before anyone else sees the wear. That's a dedication tested in private and kept running. Your account of it is that traditions carry themselves and you're just part of the room. They don't carry themselves. Someone stays with them, and that someone has their hands on the work.

Care that doesn't exhaust needs the person doing it to be visible. When the group next uses something you kept alive, leave off the line that it's nothing, and for one week where the credit sits is where it sits. What's been anonymous has an author — and the quiet upkeep stops costing you something no one, including you, was counting.
cells.sheetLine: You kept it going and called it just tradition.

attempts.check: The draft's shakiest claim is that the person is privately pressure-testing a commitment behind closed doors — the record says the crossing here is internal rather than public, but nothing supports reading their particular situation as a private contest; a reader could rightly say it's just a hard week at the group. The asks all survive being wrong because each is a small doable act (rest, give directions once, share an actual piece of help, pause before rehearsing a story) that teaches something even if the read misses. The sentence that serves me more than them is 'that thing only holds while you're defending it' — it's a bit of a wise flourish I'd want to keep, so I've cut it and said the plain version instead.
